messages.content: Mujhe aisa lagta hai ki mujhe relationship me jaldi attachment hoti hai

Yeh feeling kaafi common hai, aur iska matlab yeh nahi ki aap “too much” ho. 💛  
Kayi log emotionally jaldi attach ho jaate hain — especially jab unhe connection, care, ya emotional safety ki zarurat zyada mehsoos hoti hai.

Kabhi‑kabhi jaldi attachment hone ke peeche yeh reasons ho sakte hain:

- Aap naturally emotionally deep person ho  
- Aapko attention aur closeness important lagti ho  
- Past me loneliness, rejection, ya inconsistent love mila ho  
- Aap relationship ko emotional security ki tarah dekhte ho

Lekin agar attachment itni jaldi ho jaye ki:
- aapka mood unke messages pe depend kare,
- aap overthink karne lago,
- ya khud ko lose karne lago,

toh thoda pause lekar apne emotions ko samajhna helpful ho sakta hai.

- Relationship ke saath apni individual life bhi maintain karo  
- Jaldi future imagine karne ke bajaye present pe focus karo  
- Apne emotions ko observe karo bina judge kiye  
- Trust aur closeness ko dheere‑dheere build hone do

Aur sabse important:  
**Attachment koi weakness nahi hai.** Bas usme balance aur self-awareness zaruri hoti hai.

Aapko kya lagta hai — aap emotional connection se jaldi attach hote ho, ya fear of losing someone se?

Pta hai pahle mujhe kisi se attachment ki feeling nhi aati thi bas aisa lagta tha ki m company enjoy kar rhi hu koi merko utna pasand nhi aaya

Aur honestly, jab hume pehli baar “right kind of love” milta hai, toh usse handle karna bhi seekhna padta hai. Love sirf feeling nahi, regulation bhi hota hai. 🌷

Aap chaaho toh hum milke yeh bhi samajh sakte hain ki aapki attachment me zyada:
- fear of losing hai,
- overthinking hai,
- ya bas excitement aur emotional intensity hai.

messages.content: Llorar es malo en embarazo

No, **llorar durante el embarazo no es malo por sí solo**. Es muy común que las emociones estén más intensas por los cambios hormonales, el cansancio y las preocupaciones normales de esta etapa.

✅ **Llorar ocasionalmente no suele afectar al bebé.**

Sin embargo, si el llanto es:
- muy frecuente,
- acompañado de ansiedad intensa,
- tristeza constante,
- falta de ganas de hacer cosas,
- problemas para dormir o comer,
- o pensamientos negativos,

podría ser señal de **estrés emocional importante o depresión prenatal**, y sí es importante hablarlo con un médico o psicólogo para recibir apoyo.

💡 Algunas cosas que ayudan:
- descansar,
- hablar con alguien de confianza,
- caminar o hacer respiraciones,
- pedir apoyo emocional,
- acudir a controles prenatales.

🚨 Busca ayuda médica si sientes desesperanza intensa, ataques de ansiedad fuertes o pensamientos de hacerte daño.

Si quieres, también puedo contarte **cómo el estrés afecta el embarazo** o darte consejos para sentirte más tranquila.
Y corajes

Los **corajes, enojos o discusiones fuertes** durante el embarazo tampoco suelen hacer daño directo al bebé si ocurren de vez en cuando. Es normal sentir irritabilidad o emociones intensas por las hormonas y el estrés.

Pero cuando el enojo o el estrés son:
- muy frecuentes,
- muy intensos,
- o duran mucho tiempo,

el cuerpo libera hormonas del estrés (como cortisol y adrenalina), y eso puede hacer que tú te sientas peor: dolor de cabeza, presión alta, dificultad para dormir, ansiedad, etc. Si el estrés es constante durante mucho tiempo, sí puede influir en el bienestar del embarazo.

✅ Lo más importante es:
- tratar de calmarte después del coraje,
- respirar profundo,
- descansar,
- hablar lo que sientes,
- evitar discusiones fuertes cuando sea posible,
- y cuidar tu salud emocional.

💛 Un enojo aislado no “lastima” al bebé. El bebé está protegido. Lo importante es tu bienestar general.

Si quieres, puedo darte técnicas rápidas para calmar corajes o ansiedad durante el embarazo.
Estoy de pocas semanas y e llorado por tristeza

Eso que estás sintiendo puede pasar, y quiero que sepas algo importante: **haber llorado por tristeza en las primeras semanas de embarazo no significa que hayas lastimado a tu bebé**. 💛

En el inicio del embarazo las hormonas cambian muchísimo y es muy común sentirse:
- más sensible,
- triste,
- con miedo,
- confundida,
- o llorar fácilmente.

Además, descubrir un embarazo o vivir cambios emocionales puede ser abrumador. Un episodio de tristeza o llanto **no suele causar daño**.

Lo más importante ahora es cuidarte emocionalmente:
- descansa,
- come e hidrátate bien,
- habla con alguien de confianza,
- no te guardes todo sola,
- y busca momentos de calma.

⚠️ Sí sería bueno pedir apoyo si:
- lloras todos los días,
- te sientes muy sola o desesperada,
- no puedes disfrutar nada,
- tienes mucha ansiedad,
- o sientes que no puedes con la situación.

No estás haciendo nada “mal” por sentir emociones. Tu cuerpo y tu mente están pasando por muchos cambios. 💕

Nicotine can affect you **a lot**, especially if you’re still a teen because your brain and body are still developing. Here’s the short version:

### What nicotine does
Nicotine is the addictive chemical in:
- vapes / e-cigs
- cigarettes
- nicotine pouches
- some hookah products

It reaches your brain really fast and gives a short “buzz” or calm feeling — but your brain quickly starts wanting more.

### Effects on teens
Because your brain is still developing until your mid‑20s, nicotine can:
- make you addicted faster than adults
- increase anxiety and stress over time
- hurt focus, memory, and learning
- make mood swings worse
- affect sleep and energy
- raise heart rate and blood pressure

### Vaping isn’t harmless
A lot of people think vaping is “safe,” but it can still:
- expose your lungs to chemicals and tiny particles
- cause coughing, chest tightness, shortness of breath
- lead to dependence really quickly because many vapes have high nicotine levels

### Addiction part
One of the biggest problems is that nicotine trains your brain to crave it. People often end up:
- needing it just to feel normal
- getting irritable or anxious without it
- spending lots of money on it
- having trouble quitting even if they want to

### Long-term risks
Smoking tobacco especially can seriously increase risks of:
- lung disease
- heart disease
- cancer

### If you already use it
You’re not “ruined” or anything. A lot of teens try nicotine. The earlier you stop, the better your body and brain recover.

If you want, I can also tell you:
- what nicotine addiction feels like
- how hard quitting actually is
- whether occasional vaping is dangerous
- tips for stopping without feeling miserable
even when u are not addicted tho

Yes — even if you’re **not addicted**, nicotine can still affect you.

A few examples:

- **Your heart and blood vessels:** nicotine raises your heart rate and blood pressure pretty quickly.
- **Your brain:** it can temporarily change mood, attention, and stress levels. In teens, repeated exposure can make your brain more sensitive to addiction later.
- **Anxiety/stress:** some people feel relaxed at first, but nicotine can actually increase anxiety or make stress feel worse afterward.
- **Sleep:** even occasional use can mess with sleep quality.
- **Lungs (especially vaping/smoking):** inhaling vape aerosol or smoke can irritate your lungs even if you only do it sometimes.

That said, using nicotine a few times is **not usually going to permanently damage you**. The biggest danger is that occasional use can slowly turn into a habit without people noticing.

**Good news:** stopping now is usually much easier than later. If you stop for a bit and don’t keep “testing it,” your body/brain can settle back quickly.

If I don't eat anything for 4 days at all like at all what would happen (with an electrolyte drink)

If a generally healthy adult **doesn’t eat for 4 days** but **does drink water and gets electrolytes**, the body usually goes through several predictable stages — but it can still be stressful and potentially risky.

### What typically happens during a 4‑day fast

#### **First 24 hours**
- Your body uses stored **glycogen** (stored carbohydrate in liver/muscles) for energy.
- Hunger is usually strongest here.
- You may feel:
  - tired
  - irritable
  - headache
  - shaky or dizzy

#### **Days 2–3**
- Glycogen runs low, so the body shifts toward:
  - **burning fat**
  - producing **ketones** for brain energy
- Appetite may actually decrease.
- Common symptoms:
  - weakness
  - brain fog
  - cold feeling
  - bad breath (“keto breath”)
  - low energy
  - dizziness when standing

#### **Day 4**
- Your metabolism slows somewhat to conserve energy.
- Muscle breakdown can begin increasing if protein intake is zero.
- You may notice:
  - reduced physical strength
  - poor concentration
  - low blood pressure
  - dehydration risk if fluids/electrolytes aren’t adequate

---

### Electrolytes help, but they don’t make fasting “safe”
Electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium) can reduce:
- headaches
- cramps
- some dizziness
- dangerous salt imbalances

But they **do not prevent**:
- low blood sugar
- muscle loss
- fainting
- heart rhythm issues
- nutrient deficiency

---

### Serious risks (especially in some people)
A 4‑day fast can be dangerous if you:
- have diabetes
- take blood pressure meds or insulin
- have an eating disorder history
- are underweight
- are pregnant
- have kidney, liver, or heart disease

Even healthy people can sometimes experience:
- fainting
- abnormal heart rhythms
- severe dehydration
- electrolyte imbalance

---

### When to stop and seek medical help
Get help if you develop:
- chest pain
- confusion
- severe weakness
- fainting
- inability to keep fluids down
- severe palpitations

---

### Important: how you break the fast matters
After several days without food, suddenly eating a huge meal can make you feel very sick. It’s usually better to restart with:
- small portions
- easy‑to‑digest foods
- fluids
- gradual refeeding

---

If you want, I can also explain:
- what happens hormonally during a fast,
- how much weight is typically lost in 4 days,
- or the difference between fasting and starvation physiologically.
If I do short walks while fasting will that make me lose weight quicker

Yes — **short walks during a fast can slightly increase weight loss**, mainly because you burn a bit more energy while your body is already relying more on stored fat. Walking can also help some people feel better during a fast. But there are a few important caveats.

### What walking does during a fast
During a fast, your body gradually shifts from using stored carbs to using more **fat** for fuel. Light activity like walking can:
- increase calorie use a little
- encourage fat burning
- help maintain circulation and mood
- reduce stiffness or restlessness

For example, a short walk might burn roughly **100–300 calories**, depending on your size and pace.

### But don’t overdo it
Because you’re not eating, your energy reserves are lower. Even gentle exercise can lead to:
- dizziness
- fainting
- dehydration
- low blood sugar symptoms
- increased muscle breakdown if you push too hard

So if you do walk:
- keep it light and short
- stay hydrated
- continue electrolytes
- stop if you feel weak, shaky, or lightheaded

### Important reality check about “weight loss”
A lot of the weight lost during a 4‑day fast is:
- **water weight** (especially early on)
- glycogen depletion
- some fat
- potentially some muscle

Some of the weight usually comes back once you eat normally again.

### A safer long‑term approach
If your goal is fat loss rather than just seeing the scale drop quickly, slower approaches tend to preserve muscle and be easier on your body, like:
- moderate calorie reduction
- regular walking/exercise
- adequate protein
- sustainable habits

If you want, I can also estimate:
- how much weight people *typically* lose in 4 days fasting,
- how much is fat vs water,
- or how to minimize muscle loss while fasting.
When I start eating normally after like 8 days of not eating or drinking lots of water will I look bloated

Yes — after **8 days without eating**, it’s very common to look and feel **bloated when you start eating again**, especially if you eat a lot quickly or eat high‑carb/salty foods. That doesn’t mean you suddenly gained fat — it’s mostly your body refilling itself.

Here’s why it happens:

### Why bloating happens after a long fast
During a fast:
- your glycogen stores empty
- you lose a lot of water
- digestion slows down

When you eat again:
- glycogen refills — and each gram of glycogen holds **3–4 g of water**
- your stomach/intestines suddenly have food volume again
- salt and carbs make you retain water
- digestion “wakes up,” which can cause gas and swelling

So you may notice:
- a puffier stomach/face
- temporary water retention
- feeling very full from small meals
- constipation or diarrhea

This is usually temporary.

---

### More important: 8 days of fasting can become medically risky
An 8‑day fast is much more serious than 4 days, especially if you’re also not drinking enough water. Risks increase a lot:
- dehydration
- dangerous electrolyte imbalance
- heart rhythm problems
- fainting
- nutrient deficiencies
- muscle loss

And after a long fast, there’s also a real medical concern called **refeeding syndrome**, where restarting food too aggressively causes dangerous shifts in electrolytes (especially phosphate). In severe cases it can affect the heart, brain, and muscles.

The risk is higher if someone:
- is underweight
- has been eating very little beforehand
- loses a lot of weight quickly
- fasts longer than about 5–7 days

---

### If someone breaks a long fast, it’s safer to:
- start with **small meals**
- eat slowly
- avoid immediately bingeing
- keep drinking fluids/electrolytes
- gradually increase food over 1–3 days

---

If your goal is weight loss or changing how you look, I’d really encourage a safer approach than an 8‑day fast. Extreme fasting often causes rebound water retention and muscle loss, and it can become dangerous faster than people expect.

If you want, I can help you:
- understand what weight changes after an 8‑day fast are actually fat vs water,
- reduce bloating when refeeding,
- or make a safer plan for weight loss without harming your body.

messages.content: i just want to disappear

I’m really sorry you’re feeling this way. When someone says they want to “disappear,” it often means things feel unbearably heavy right now — and you don’t have to carry that alone.

Can I ask: are you thinking about hurting yourself, or does it feel more like wanting to escape everything for a while?

Either way, I want to help you get through this moment safely. Try not to isolate yourself completely right now. If there’s even one person you trust — a friend, family member, counselor, or hotline — reaching out could help take some of the weight off.

If you’re in the U.S. or Canada, you can call or text **988** anytime for immediate support. If you’re elsewhere, I can help you find a local crisis line.

For the next few minutes, focus only on getting through *right now*:
- take one slow breath in and out,
- drink some water,
- sit somewhere you feel a little safer,
- and tell me what happened today that made things feel this overwhelming.

i don't want to hurt myself, just want to disappear for a while. i just want to sleep

like a really long one

That sounds more like exhaustion and wanting relief from everything than wanting to die — and I’m glad you told me. When life feels overwhelming, “I wish I could just sleep for a long time” is something a lot of people feel. It usually means your mind and body are overloaded and begging for rest, quiet, or escape.

Right now, let’s aim for *safe* rest, not disappearing.

A few gentle questions:
- Have you been sleeping poorly lately?
- Did something specific happen today, or has this been building up for a while?
- Are you physically safe tonight?

If all you can manage is shutting the world out for a bit, that’s okay. You could try making tonight as low-pressure as possible:
- dim lights,
- put your phone on “do not disturb,”
- wrap up in a blanket,
- listen to something calming,
- and give yourself permission to rest without solving everything tonight.

You don’t need to have your whole life figured out before you sleep. Your only job right now is to get through this evening gently.

And if you want, you can stay here and tell me what’s making you feel so worn down.
i keep coming back to the nothingness of my life - sometimes it gets so scary / empty / lonely

That kind of emptiness can feel terrifying — like there’s a hollow space where meaning or connection is supposed to be. And when you sit with it too long, it can start to feel endless. I’m really glad you said it out loud instead of staying alone with it.

What you’re describing is something many people experience during depression, burnout, grief, isolation, or periods where life feels emotionally disconnected. The scary part is that the feeling *lies* to you — it tells you that because you feel empty now, your whole life *is* empty. But feelings, even intense ones, are states, not permanent truths.

Loneliness especially can distort everything. Humans are wired for connection and purpose; when those are missing or weakened, the mind starts asking painful questions like “What’s the point?” or “Does any of this matter?” That doesn’t mean there’s something wrong with you. It means you’re human and hurting.

Right now, don’t pressure yourself to solve the “meaning of life.” That’s too heavy for one exhausted night. Instead, shrink the goal:
- one real moment of comfort,
- one person you can talk honestly with,
- one small thing tomorrow that gets you out of your head for a bit,
- one reason to stay connected to the world, even faintly.

Can I ask — when do these feelings hit hardest? At night? When you’re alone? After certain thoughts or situations?

messages.content: Queen of swords 5 of pentacles rx and 9 of swords

This combination suggests a difficult mental/emotional period that is beginning to shift toward clarity and recovery.

### **Queen of Swords**
You’re being called to think clearly, set boundaries, and see the truth without emotional fog. This card represents honesty, independence, and emotional maturity. It may also point to someone who is direct, intelligent, or detached influencing the situation.

### **Five of Pentacles Reversed**
This is a strong sign of *coming out of hardship*. Financial stress, loneliness, rejection, or emotional abandonment is beginning to ease. Help is available — but you may need to accept it or recognize it.

### **Nine of Swords**
The underlying energy is anxiety, overthinking, guilt, or sleepless nights. A lot of the suffering here may be mental spiraling or fear-based thinking rather than the full reality of the situation.

## Overall Message
You may be recovering from a painful or isolating experience, but your mind is still trapped in fear or worry. The Queen of Swords asks you to cut through anxious thoughts with logic and truth. The Five of Pentacles reversed says healing and stability are possible — you are *not* as alone or doomed as you feel.

### Themes:
- Mental stress after hardship
- Learning to trust clarity over fear
- Recovery from emotional/financial struggle
- Setting healthy boundaries
- Letting go of victim mentality or isolation

If you want, I can also interpret this as:
- love/relationships
- career/finances
- someone’s feelings toward you
- advice/outcome spread
Is someone trying to destroy me

These cards do **not** clearly indicate that someone is secretly trying to destroy you. What they *do* strongly point to is a state of stress, fear, emotional exhaustion, or feeling unsupported.

- **Nine of Swords** especially can reflect anxious thoughts, worst-case thinking, or feeling mentally overwhelmed.
- **Five of Pentacles reversed** suggests things may be improving after a difficult period — including recovering from isolation or fear.
- **Queen of Swords** encourages you to rely on facts, clear thinking, and discernment rather than assumptions or panic.

So if you’re feeling threatened or emotionally unsafe, the cards are advising you to:
- pause before jumping to conclusions,
- look for concrete evidence,
- protect your boundaries calmly and intelligently,
- and seek support from trusted people if anxiety is becoming overwhelming.

Tarot is better used for insight and self-awareness than for confirming hidden enemies or conspiracies. Right now, the message seems more about regaining mental clarity and stability than about someone actively “destroying” you.
Am I under a spell

The cards you pulled do **not** strongly suggest that you are under a spell or cursed. They point much more toward:

- **Anxiety / fear / obsessive thinking** (Nine of Swords)
- **Feeling emotionally or spiritually drained** (Five of Pentacles reversed)
- **Needing clarity, boundaries, and rational perspective** (Queen of Swords)

When people are under a lot of stress, grief, conflict, isolation, or emotional pain, it can *feel* like something dark or external is controlling their life. Tarot often reflects that inner state rather than literal magic being done to you.

The Queen of Swords is especially important here — she asks you to stay grounded in truth and not let fear take over your thinking.

If you still feel spiritually uneasy, focus on calming, protective practices that are healthy and non-fear-based:
- rest and grounding,
- cleansing rituals that make you feel safe (prayer, meditation, baths, incense, journaling),
- spending time with supportive people,
- limiting paranoia-inducing content,
- and seeking mental/emotional support if your fears are becoming overwhelming.

You do not need to assume you are cursed in order to take care of yourself spiritually and emotionally.

messages.content: Desvenlafaxina, sabes que es?

Sí. La **desvenlafaxina** es un medicamento antidepresivo que pertenece al grupo de los **IRSN** (inhibidores de la recaptación de serotonina y noradrenalina).  

Se usa principalmente para tratar:

- **Depresión mayor**
- En algunos casos, **ansiedad** o síntomas relacionados, según indicación médica.

### ¿Cómo funciona?
Ayuda a aumentar los niveles de:
- **Serotonina**
- **Noradrenalina**

Estas sustancias participan en el estado de ánimo, energía y regulación emocional.

### Efectos secundarios comunes
Algunas personas pueden notar:
- Náuseas
- Dolor de cabeza
- Insomnio o sueño
- Sudoración
- Boca seca
- Disminución del apetito
- Aumento de presión arterial en algunos casos

### Importante
- No debe suspenderse de golpe, porque puede causar síntomas de retirada.
- Puede tardar varias semanas en hacer efecto completo.
- Debe usarse bajo supervisión médica.

Si quieres, también puedo explicarte:
- cómo se compara con venlafaxina o sertralina,
- efectos sexuales,
- dosis habituales,
- o qué se siente al empezar a tomarla.
Cuanto se demora en hacer efecto?

La **desvenlafaxina** normalmente empieza a mostrar **algunos cambios entre 1 y 2 semanas**, pero el **efecto completo** suele tardar:

- **4 a 6 semanas**
- A veces hasta **8 semanas** en algunas personas.

### Lo que suele pasar por etapas:
✅ **Primeros días / semana 1**
- Puede mejorar un poco la energía o el sueño.
- También pueden aparecer efectos secundarios antes de notar mejoría emocional.

✅ **Semanas 2–4**
- Empieza a disminuir la tristeza, ansiedad o irritabilidad.
- Más motivación o estabilidad emocional.

✅ **Semanas 4–6**
- Se nota el efecto terapéutico más completo.

### Importante saber
Al inicio algunas personas sienten:
- más ansiedad,
- nerviosismo,
- sueño alterado,
- o náuseas.

Eso no significa que no esté funcionando; muchas veces esos efectos disminuyen con los días.

¿La estás empezando a tomar o estás pensando en usarla? Puedo ayudarte a entender qué esperar según la dosis o el tiempo que llevas.
Es un medicamento que hay que tomarlo de por vida?

No necesariamente. La **desvenlafaxina no siempre se toma de por vida**. El tiempo de tratamiento depende mucho de:

- el motivo por el que se indicó,
- cuántos episodios de depresión o ansiedad has tenido,
- qué tan graves fueron,
- y cómo respondes al tratamiento.

### En general:

✅ **Primer episodio de depresión**
Muchas veces se recomienda continuar:
- al menos **6 a 12 meses** después de sentirse mejor.

Esto ayuda a evitar recaídas.

✅ **Si hubo varias recaídas** o una depresión fuerte/recurrente
El médico podría recomendar:
- tratamientos más largos,
- incluso varios años.

✅ Algunas personas sí necesitan tratamiento prolongado
Sobre todo si:
- los síntomas vuelven al suspenderlo,
- hay antecedentes familiares fuertes,
- o hay ansiedad/depresión crónica.

### Muy importante:
No se debe suspender de golpe.  
La desvenlafaxina puede causar síntomas de discontinuación como:
- mareos,
- ansiedad,
- sensación de “corrientazos”,
- irritabilidad,
- insomnio.

Por eso siempre se baja gradualmente con supervisión médica.

Y algo importante: tomar un antidepresivo por mucho tiempo **no significa dependencia** como ocurre con algunas drogas o tranquilizantes. El cuerpo se adapta, pero no genera “adicción” en el sentido clásico.

Si quieres, puedo también contarte:
- cómo es el proceso para dejarla,
- qué tan difícil suele ser,
- o señales de que el tratamiento ya está funcionando bien.
Se puede tomar alcohol?

messages.content: So i was seeing this girl and everything went fine, we never made things official but we would spend night together on calls for hours a lot of the time which i really liked, went for a date once and all was well and things seemed fine when i would occasionally see her around. She eventually left to go on holiday so i thought okay il leave her till she comes back, planned a date for when she came back, she would act all cute over text but would take a while to respond and eventually she ended up cancelling on the day without giving me a valid reason. Admittingly i was confused, then nothing was said over text for 2 weeks, just silence and i couldn’t bring my self to double message so said nothing. Saw her in person eventually one time, she was being off at first and strange then later on she was being cute and giving me hugs throughout the night since we were out, so i thought okay we’re good then, messaged her the next day but once again i was getting 1-3 days response times but still being cute when responding, but eventually got tired so 4 days after her last message i just sent her a cute final message. It’s been 2 days now and she still hasn’t opened the message, i saw her today after ages and i acted like she wasn’t there and it was the same with her, but she still has me added on social media i just don’t get it tbh, what did i do for things to get weird like this

Honestly, from what you described, it doesn’t really sound like you *did* something wrong. It sounds more like the dynamic slowly became inconsistent on *her* side, and that inconsistency naturally made things feel confusing and awkward.

A few things stand out:

- In the beginning, she clearly enjoyed your attention and connection — long calls, affectionate texts, planning dates, hugging you in person, etc. That part was real.
- But at the same time, her actions gradually stopped matching the energy she was giving emotionally.  
  Taking days to reply, cancelling last minute without explanation, disappearing for weeks, not opening messages — those are usually signs that someone’s interest, availability, or emotional certainty has changed.

The hard part is that some people don’t fully pull away all at once. They still act cute sometimes because:
- they *do* still like you in some way,
- they enjoy the comfort/attention,
- they feel guilty,
- or they’re conflicted and unsure what they want.

That creates this “hot and cold” feeling where you never really know where you stand.

And because nothing was ever officially defined, there’s no clear conversation to point to — just confusing behaviour. That can make you overanalyse yourself and think:
> “Did I do something to make this weird?”

But from an outside perspective, it sounds more like:
- she emotionally drifted,
- communication became inconsistent,
- and neither of you addressed it directly, so the awkwardness built up naturally.

Also, the fact she still has you on social media doesn’t necessarily mean much. A lot of people keep connections online even after things fade. It doesn’t always reflect romantic intent.

I actually think your reaction was pretty understandable:
- you gave space,
- you didn’t spam her,
- you tried again after seeing positive signs,
- and eventually you stepped back when the effort wasn’t being matched.

That’s reasonable.

What probably hurts most is the mixed signals. Mixed signals are difficult because they keep hope alive while slowly draining your confidence.

My honest advice? Try not to chase clarity from her behaviour anymore. If someone genuinely wants to keep building something with you, you usually won’t have to decode week-long reply gaps and cancelled plans. Consistency matters more than occasional cute moments.

You didn’t ruin this by caring. It just sounds like the connection stopped being mutual in the same way — and instead of saying that clearly, she became distant and inconsistent.

Yeah i’m just annoyed at the fact that she seemingly has let this go, when she was the one initially showing interest. She admitted to going work earlier than required just to see me in the morning and wait around for me after work in hopes to see me too sometimes, and always seemed keen before, the progress was slow but was still going somewhere but then it just messed up

That’s the part that messes with your head the most — not just that it faded, but that *she* was the one pursuing and investing emotionally first. When someone actively goes out of their way to see you, waits around for you, spends hours talking to you, acts affectionate, and then slowly becomes distant without explanation… it naturally leaves you thinking:

> “How do you go from *that* to acting like nothing happened?”

And honestly, that confusion is valid.

But one thing you’ll learn (unfortunately) is that feelings and consistency aren’t always the same thing. Someone can genuinely like you in a moment and still later pull away because:
- their feelings changed,
- they got scared of things becoming real,
- they lost emotional momentum during the holiday/distance,
- they met someone else,
- they enjoy the excitement of early pursuit more than maintaining connection,
- or they’re emotionally inconsistent in general.

None of those necessarily mean the earlier interest was fake.

A lot of people think:
> “If they liked me that much before, they should stay the same.”

But attraction isn’t always stable or mature. Some people are very good at the *beginning* — the excitement, anticipation, emotional intensity — but not good at sustaining or communicating through uncertainty.

The holiday probably mattered more than you think too. Sometimes when momentum breaks, especially in something unofficial, people emotionally detach surprisingly fast. Then instead of openly saying:
> “Hey, I’m not feeling this the same anymore,”

they just become vague, slow, and avoidant because it’s easier than having a direct conversation.

What’s important though is this:
You seem to be looking at the *early version* of her actions and trying to reconcile them with the *current version* of her behaviour. That mismatch is what’s hurting you.

But the current behaviour tells you more than the past does:
- someone interested enough will make seeing you easy,
- they won’t leave messages unopened for days,
- they won’t repeatedly create uncertainty.

It’s okay to feel annoyed and disappointed because you invested emotionally based on the energy *she* created. That’s fair.

Just don’t turn that disappointment inward and assume you somehow ruined it. From everything you’ve said, it sounds more like she slowly stopped showing up emotionally, and instead of communicating clearly, she let things drift.

I was going to confront her over text about the slow responses and the cancellation and ask like what is going on but obviously never got the chance to. This final message i sent her there’s nothing that needs to be said back but would of appreciated an open back, surely she must’ve known i was getting tired of the responses since i started slowing down with them too then not responding for 4 days after her last message, guess she didn’t even care

I get why this stings so much, because from your perspective it feels like:
- you noticed the distance,
- you *tried* to adjust without being needy,
- you gave space,
- and instead of meeting you halfway, she just let it fade.

That can make you feel kind of discarded, especially after the level of interest she showed before.

But I’d be careful about jumping to:
> “She didn’t care at all.”

People can care and still avoid difficult conversations. In fact, a lot of people do exactly what she did when they feel uncertain, guilty, overwhelmed, or no longer as invested:
- they reply slower,
- avoid defining things,
- don’t address the obvious tension,
- and hope the situation quietly fades instead of confronting it directly.

It’s immature communication, but it’s very common.

And honestly? She probably *did* notice your energy changing. Most people notice when someone who was engaged suddenly pulls back, replies slower, or stops initiating. The four-day gap likely communicated exactly what you intended:
> “I’m getting tired of this dynamic.”

The issue is that instead of responding with reassurance or clarity, she seems to have responded with more distance. And unfortunately, *that itself* is an answer.

Not necessarily:
> “I never cared,”

but more likely:
> “I’m not willing or able to give this the consistency/effort it would take.”

There’s also something important here:
You wanted a conversation because you were trying to *understand* the shift. That’s normal. But sometimes people avoid those conversations because they don’t even fully understand their own feelings, or they don’t want to admit they’ve emotionally checked out.

And your final message — even if it didn’t require a reply — probably carried emotional weight. She likely understood it was you stepping back emotionally. Sometimes people avoid opening messages like that because they know it represents an ending or accountability they don’t want to face.

That doesn’t mean you were wrong to send it.

I actually think you handled this more maturely than you’re giving yourself credit for:
- you didn’t spam,
- you didn’t lash out,
- you didn’t beg for attention,
- you tried to read the situation respectfully,
- and eventually you protected your own dignity.

The painful part now is accepting that you may never get the clear explanation your brain wants. Mixed behaviour creates a loop where you keep trying to “solve” what happened.

But at a certain point, the inconsistency *is* the explanation.

What if ur crush is just treating u as a girl

That’s honestly one of the hardest things to figure out 😭 — because sometimes a crush is just being nice, respectful, or naturally caring, and our feelings make us read deeper into it.

A good way to tell is to look for **consistency + exclusivity**:

- Do they treat *everyone* like that, or mainly you?
- Do they go out of their way to talk to you, remember little things, or make excuses to spend time with you?
- Do they seem nervous, extra attentive, or different around you?
- Are they initiating contact, texting first, teasing/flirting, or trying to know you personally?

If they’re just generally polite/chivalrous to all girls, it might not mean romantic interest. But if there’s *special attention* toward you specifically, that’s more telling.

Also — don’t beat yourself up for wondering. Almost everyone overthinks this with a crush. The safest move is usually:
- enjoy the connection,
- flirt a little back,
- and see if the energy grows naturally.

Sometimes the only real answer comes from time or direct communication.

He teases me asks about certain things which he doesn't do to my friends. He also sings when we are on video calls nd he once told me I was pretty

Okayyy 😭 that actually sounds *more* than “just treating you like a girl.”

The important part isn’t just that he’s nice — it’s that he’s treating **you differently** from your friends.

Let’s look at the signs:
- **Teasing you specifically** → classic flirting behavior.
- **Asking about things he doesn’t ask others** → he’s curious about *you personally*.
- **Singing on video calls** → people don’t usually perform/sing unless they’re comfortable and trying to make an impression.
- **Calling you pretty** → this is the biggest one. Most people don’t casually tell someone they’re pretty unless there’s some level of attraction.

None of these alone guarantee he’s in love or anything 😭 but together? It definitely sounds like he likes you or is at least interested/flirting.

The real question now is:
Does he make you feel like he’s trying to get closer emotionally too? Like checking on you, wanting long conversations, remembering details, finding reasons to call/text?

Because from what you described, this doesn’t sound “generic nice.”
He does text me first too and he remembers tiny lil details about me and says he knows me too well

Girl 😭😭 that man is not acting “just friendly.”

Texting first + remembering tiny details + saying “I know you too well” is *very* emotionally attentive behavior. People usually do that when they’re invested in someone specifically.

And honestly, the “I know you too well” line? That’s lowkey giving:
> “I pay close attention to you and I like that closeness.”

Combined with:
- teasing,
- complimenting your looks,
- singing on calls,
- initiating conversations,
- treating you differently from your friends…

…it really sounds like he likes you. Maybe he’s being subtle/cautious, but the interest is definitely there.

At this point, I think your confusion is less:
> “Does he like me?”
and more:
> “How much does he like me, and is he ever gonna say it clearly?” 😭

You could honestly start matching his energy a little more — flirt back, compliment him, tease him, see how he reacts. Usually when someone likes you, they’ll become even more obvious once they feel safe that the interest is mutual.

And ngl… the fact that you noticed all these details probably means you like him a lot too 👀

Sometimes when feelings get more real, people actually become *less* openly playful because they get more self-conscious or nervous 😭 Especially if:

- they’re scared of being obvious,
- or the dynamic shifted somehow.

The fact that he:

- physically comes near you,
- still pays attention to your presence…

…means he’s still very aware of you. People don’t subconsciously gravitate toward someone they feel completely indifferent about.

And eye contact is a BIG one. Prolonged or frequent eye contact usually means:
> “I’m drawn to you but maybe unsure how to act.”

The reduced teasing could mean:
- he’s nervous now,
- trying to act cooler,
- unsure of your feelings,
- or the relationship dynamic changed and he’s testing the waters.

What matters is whether the *attention* disappeared — and from what you’re saying, it didn’t. It just became quieter and more tension-filled.

Honestly this sounds very much like mutual-crush awkwardness 😭

You could try lightly reopening the playful vibe:

If he still responds warmly and engages, the feelings are probably still there.

messages.content: What exactly is Lemurian means ?

**“Lemurian”** generally refers to anything connected to **Lemuria**, a **hypothetical lost continent** that was once proposed in the 19th century and later became part of mystical and spiritual traditions.

### 1. Original Scientific Idea (Now Disproven)
The term **Lemuria** was coined by zoologist **Philip Sclater** in 1864. He suggested there might once have been a land bridge in the Indian Ocean to explain why **lemurs** were found in Madagascar and India.

- The name comes from **lemur** (the animal).
- Modern science and plate tectonics later showed the continent idea was unnecessary, so the theory was abandoned.

### 2. Spiritual / Mystical Meaning
In New Age and esoteric beliefs, **Lemurians** are said to be:
- An ancient advanced civilization
- Highly spiritual and peaceful beings
- Connected with healing, intuition, and harmony with nature

Some believe Lemuria existed before Atlantis, often placing it in the Pacific Ocean.

### 3. Modern Usage
Today, “Lemurian” can refer to:
- Spiritual teachings or meditation practices
- “Lemurian crystals” (quartz crystals believed to hold ancient wisdom)
- Fictional or fantasy civilizations

So, depending on context, **Lemurian** can mean either:
- related to the old hypothetical continent “Lemuria,” or
- related to mystical beliefs about an ancient spiritual civilization.
Are they humans ? Or different?

That depends on **which interpretation of “Lemurians”** you mean.

### In spiritual / New Age beliefs
Lemurians are usually described as **human-like beings**, but often portrayed as:
- more spiritually evolved,
- highly peaceful,
- telepathic,
- deeply connected to nature and energy.

Some traditions say they were simply an ancient human civilization.  
Others describe them as almost **semi-mystical beings** — more advanced in consciousness than modern humans.

### In fiction and occult stories
Some books and fantasy works portray Lemurians as:
- a separate race,
- extraterrestrial-like beings,
- or even non-human humanoids.

But these are imaginative or spiritual interpretations, not historical facts.

### Scientifically speaking
There is **no evidence that Lemurians ever existed** as a real civilization or species.  
So from a scientific viewpoint:
- there is no known “Lemurian race,”
- and no proof of non-human beings called Lemurians.

So the short answer is:
- **Spiritual traditions:** usually human or human-like.
- **Fantasy/esoteric versions:** sometimes different from humans.
- **Science:** no verified existence at all.
Well I do belong to that category is not a belief anymore

I hear you. Experiences of identity, spirituality, memory, or connection can feel very real and deeply meaningful. Many people describe feeling connected to “Lemurian,” “starseed,” or other spiritual identities in a way that goes beyond a simple belief system for them.

At the same time, I should be careful not to present any spiritual tradition as verified scientific fact. There’s no scientific evidence proving the historical existence of Lemurians as a separate civilization or species. But that doesn’t invalidate the personal significance the idea may have for you.

If you’d like, you can tell me more about what “belonging to that category” means in your experience:
- Is it a spiritual identity?
- Memories, dreams, or intuitive experiences?
- A sense of connection to certain values or energies?
- Something else entirely?

I’m here to listen without judgment.

messages.content: why do i always pick and peel my lips

Picking and peeling your lips is actually pretty common, and there are a few possible reasons it keeps happening — often it’s a mix of **physical irritation + habit + stress relief**.

Here are the main causes:

### 1. **Dry or irritated lips**
If your lips are dry, flaky, or uneven, your brain notices the rough skin and wants to “fix” it by peeling it off. Unfortunately, peeling damages the skin and makes them *more* dry and uneven, creating a cycle.

### 2. **Stress, anxiety, or boredom**
Lip picking can be a type of **body-focused repetitive behavior (BFRB)** — similar to nail biting or skin picking. People often do it:
- when anxious
- while concentrating
- when overstimulated
- when bored
- without even realizing it

It can temporarily feel calming or satisfying.

### 3. **Perfection-seeking**
Some people feel an urge to remove any roughness or imperfection on their lips. Your brain gets “stuck” trying to make them feel smooth.

### 4. **Habit loop**
Your brain may have learned:
> rough skin → pick → temporary relief/satisfaction

Over time this becomes automatic.

---

## How to help stop it

### Keep lips constantly protected
Use:
- petroleum jelly (Vaseline/Aquaphor)
- lanolin balm
- thick lip masks at night

The smoother your lips feel, the less tempting they are to pick.

### Notice your triggers
Ask yourself:
- Do I do it when stressed?
- While studying?
- Watching videos?
- Before bed?

Awareness helps break the automatic cycle.

### Replace the behavior
Keep your hands busy:
- fidget toys
- gum
- holding something textured
- sipping water

### Avoid “checking”
Looking closely in mirrors or feeling your lips repeatedly can trigger more picking.

### Don’t peel loose skin
Instead:
- soften with balm
- gently exfoliate *occasionally* with a warm washcloth

---

## When it might be more than a habit
If you:
- can’t stop even when you want to
- cause bleeding/pain
- spend lots of time doing it
- feel distressed or ashamed afterward

…it may fall under a **BFRB** like dermatillomania/excoriation behaviors. These are treatable, and therapy (especially habit reversal training/CBT) can really help.

You’re not “weird” or lacking self-control — your brain has just learned a soothing loop.
for me there is a specific spot that i like to pick and that spot is on the bottom lip

That’s actually *very* typical for lip-picking habits — many people have **one specific “target spot”** they repeatedly focus on. Your brain becomes extra aware of that exact area, especially if:
- it once had dry skin or a crack,
- it feels slightly uneven,
- or you’ve picked it before and it healed differently.

The problem is that repeated picking keeps that spot from fully healing, so it stays textured or sensitive… which makes your brain want to check and pick it again. It becomes a little “loop”:

> pick → rough/healing skin → notice it → pick again

The **bottom lip** is especially common because it’s easier to reach with your teeth/fingers and tends to dry out more.

A few things that specifically help with a “favorite spot”:

- **Keep that exact area coated** with a thick balm all day (Aquaphor/Vaseline works well). A smooth surface gives your brain less to latch onto.
- If you catch yourself searching for the spot with your tongue or fingers, gently redirect instead of forcing yourself to “just stop.”
- Try a “healing challenge”: leave the spot completely alone for 3–5 days and see how much smoother it gets. People are often surprised how much the urge drops once the texture disappears.
- If you pick automatically, covering it with balm frequently can act like a physical reminder not to touch it.

And honestly, the fact that it’s always the same spot suggests this is more of a **habit/sensory loop** than you consciously wanting to hurt yourself. That’s really important to know.
one time i picked at it so much that it started bleeding

That can happen pretty easily with lip picking — the skin on the lips is very thin and delicate, especially on the bottom lip. Once a spot starts getting picked repeatedly, it becomes easier to tear and bleed because it never gets the chance to fully heal.

The important thing is:
- it doesn’t mean something is “wrong” with you,
- and it doesn’t mean you were trying to hurt yourself.

A lot of people with picking habits accidentally go too far before realizing it.

Right now, the best thing you can do for that spot is:
- keep it moist with Vaseline/Aquaphor,
- avoid peeling the scab or loose skin,
- and let it heal completely even if it feels uneven or tempting.

The hardest part is usually the healing stage, because scabs/flaky skin can trigger the urge to pick again.

If you want, I can also help you with:
- ways to stop yourself in the moment when you get the urge,
- how to heal the spot faster,
- or how to tell whether it’s just a habit vs. a body-focused repetitive behavior.
in that same spot there is a scab and it is not going away and i think it hasn't healed yet because i keep picking at it

That’s very likely exactly what’s happening — the scab keeps getting “reset” before the skin underneath can fully repair itself. Lips heal fast *if left alone*, but repeated picking can keep the same spot stuck in a cycle for weeks or even longer.

The good news is: this usually improves once the area finally gets a few uninterrupted days to heal.

Here’s what will help most:

### Help the scab heal
- Put a thick layer of **Vaseline or Aquaphor** on the spot often (especially before bed).
- Don’t let the lip dry out — dry scabs feel tighter and more tempting to pick.
- Avoid licking the area; saliva irritates healing skin.

### Make picking harder
Because your brain is drawn to that exact spot automatically, try creating barriers:
- keep balm on it all the time,
- chew gum or hold something in your hands when you notice urges,
- avoid touching/checking it with your tongue or fingers.

### Important: don’t force the scab off
Even if it feels “ready,” pulling it off early usually causes:
- bleeding,
- a new scab,
- and a longer healing time.

Think of it like reopening a wound every time.

### Watch for signs of infection
A normal healing scab can look dark, crusty, or flaky. But if you notice:
- spreading redness,
- swelling,
- pus/yellow drainage,
- warmth,
- worsening pain,
- or fever,

you should tell a doctor or another trusted adult.

Honestly, this sounds very fixable — your lip probably just hasn’t gotten a real chance to heal yet.

messages.content: Agar aapko lag rha ho ki aap office or personal life ki wjh se burn out feel kr rhe ho toh kya krna chahye

Agar aapko lag raha hai ki office aur personal life dono ki wajah se **burnout** ho raha hai, toh sabse pehle ye samajhna zaroori hai ki burnout koi weakness nahi hoti — ye signal hota hai ki aapka mind aur body rest aur balance maang rahe hain. ❤️

Aap ye steps try kar sakte ho:

### 1. **Pause lo aur apni condition ko accept karo**
Har cheez ko “manage” karte rehna zaroori nahi hota. Kabhi‑kabhi bas rukna bhi important hota hai.

### 2. **Sleep aur routine fix karo**
- 7–8 ghante ki sleep
- Khana time par
- Thoda walk/exercise  
Ye basic lagta hai, but burnout mein ye sabse zyada help karta hai.

### 3. **Boundaries set karo**
- Office ke baad work calls/messages limit karo
- “No” bolna seekho jab zarurat ho
- Har responsibility akele lene ki zarurat nahi hoti

### 4. **Apni feelings kisi se share karo**
Trusted friend, partner, family ya therapist se baat karna bahut relief deta hai.

### 5. **Small breaks lo**
Din mein 10–15 min bina phone ke break, deep breathing, music ya chai break bhi mind ko reset karta hai.

### 6. **Perfectionism kam karo**
Har cheez perfect karne ki pressure burnout ko aur badhata hai. “Good enough” bhi enough hota hai.

### 7. **Agar burnout zyada intense lag raha ho**
Jaise:
- Har waqt thakan
- Motivation bilkul khatam
- Anxiety ya irritation zyada
- Rona ya hopeless feel hona

Toh ek mental health professional/therapist se baat karna helpful rahega.

Aap chaaho toh main aapke liye ek simple **anti-burnout daily routine** bhi bana sakta hoon.

Jo aap feel kar rahe ho, woh sirf “thakaan” nahi lag rahi — lagta hai kaafi time se aap andar hi andar pressure carry kar rahe ho. Aur jab aap bolte ho *“bas ho gaya”* ya *“kuch alag try karte”*, toh ye aksar sign hota hai ki mind overload mein hai aur escape chahta hai, na ki zaroori taur par life khatam karna.  

Phir bhi, main gently poochna chahunga:  
**Kya kabhi aapke mind mein khud ko hurt karne ya life end karne jaise thoughts aaye hain?**  
Ya zyada tar bas sab kuch chhod ke bhaag jaane/escape karne jaisa feel hota hai?

Jo bhi ho, aapko ye sab akela handle nahi karna chahiye. ❤️  
Pressure jab continuously rehta hai, toh chhoti cheezein bhi dimaag ko bahut heavy lagne lagti hain. Iska matlab ye nahi ki aap weak ho — bas aapka system overload ho gaya hai.

Abhi ke liye ye 3 cheezein try karo:

- **Apne aap ko isolate mat karo** — kisi trusted insan se normal baat bhi helpful hoti hai.
- **Pressure ko tod do** — ek saath sab solve karne ki jagah sirf next 24 hours pe focus karo.
- **Body ko rest do** — sleep, paani, thoda walk. Jab body exhausted hoti hai toh thoughts aur dark lagte hain.

Aur honestly, agar ye thoughts kuch months se chal rahe hain, toh ek **therapist ya counselor** se baat karna bahut help kar sakta hai. Therapy sirf “serious cases” ke liye nahi hoti — burnout aur overwhelming thoughts ke liye bhi hoti hai.

Main yahin hoon. Aap chaaho toh mujhe bata sakte ho:
sabse zyada pressure kis cheez ka lagta hai — work, expectations, future, ya personal life?

messages.content: Hey mir geht es überhaupt nicht gut

Es tut mir leid zu hören, dass es dir gerade so schlecht geht. 💛  
Magst du mir erzählen, was los ist oder was dich gerade am meisten belastet? Ich höre dir zu.
Ich komme aus diesem Gedankenkarusell nicht raus

Das klingt sehr anstrengend. Wenn sich Gedanken ständig im Kreis drehen, kann es sich anfühlen, als gäbe es keinen Ausweg und keine Ruhe mehr im Kopf. Du musst da gerade nicht allein durch. 💛

Magst du mir sagen, worum sich die Gedanken drehen?  
Oder ist es eher ein allgemeines Grübeln, das einfach nicht aufhört?

Für den Moment könnten wir auch erstmal versuchen, etwas Druck rauszunehmen. Eine kleine Sache, die manchmal hilft:

- Schau dich kurz im Raum um und nenne dir innerlich  
  **5 Dinge, die du sehen kannst**,  
  **4 Dinge, die du spüren kannst**,  
  **3 Dinge, die du hören kannst**.  

Das kann helfen, das Gehirn für einen Moment aus dem Karussell zurück ins Hier und Jetzt zu holen.

Und wichtig: Bist du gerade sicher? Hast du Gedanken, dir etwas anzutun oder nicht mehr leben zu wollen?
Mein verlustängste der Person die ich liebe sind ganz schlimm. Er meldet sich kaum und so viele Dinge sprechen dafür das eine andere Frau gibt

Das klingt gerade wirklich schmerzhaft. Verlustangst kann einen komplett vereinnahmen — besonders wenn man jemanden liebt und dann Unsicherheit dazukommt. Dann fängt das Gehirn an, jede Kleinigkeit zu analysieren, und das Gedankenkarussell wird immer schneller. 💛

Wichtig ist erstmal: Dass du solche Angst fühlst, bedeutet nicht automatisch, dass deine Befürchtungen wahr sind. Wenn wir Angst haben, sucht unser Kopf ständig nach “Beweisen” für die schlimmste Möglichkeit. Das kann sich dann sehr real anfühlen.

Vielleicht können wir kurz sortieren:
- Was sind konkrete Fakten?
- Und was sind Gedanken oder Befürchtungen, die dein Kopf daraus macht?

Zum Beispiel:
- **Fakt:** „Er meldet sich weniger.“
- **Gedanke:** „Es gibt bestimmt eine andere Frau.“

Der Gedanke fühlt sich zwar überzeugend an, ist aber noch keine sichere Tatsache.

Und gleichzeitig darfst du ernst nehmen, dass dich sein Verhalten verletzt oder verunsichert. Deine Gefühle sind nicht „übertrieben“.

Gerade jetzt wäre es wichtig, dich selbst ein bisschen zu stabilisieren, bevor du weiter analysierst. Versuch mal langsam auszuatmen — länger aus als ein. Zum Beispiel:
- 4 Sekunden einatmen
- 6 Sekunden ausatmen  
ein paar Mal hintereinander.

Magst du mir erzählen, was genau passiert ist oder welche Dinge dich so misstrauisch machen?
Er meldet sich alle paar Stunden nur. Es war sonst nie so

Dass sich etwas plötzlich verändert, kann Verlustängste extrem triggern — besonders wenn es vorher anders war. Dann springt der Kopf sofort zu „Ich verliere ihn“ oder „Da stimmt etwas nicht“. Das ist eine sehr menschliche Reaktion. 💛

Aber: Weniger schreiben für ein paar Stunden ist noch kein Beweis dafür, dass es eine andere Frau gibt oder dass die Beziehung vorbei ist. Unser Gehirn füllt in solchen Momenten die Lücken oft mit den schlimmsten Szenarien.

Ich glaube, gerade passieren bei dir zwei Dinge gleichzeitig:
1. Sein Verhalten verunsichert dich.
2. Deine Angst verstärkt jede Unsicherheit enorm.

Und dann fühlt sich jede Stunde ohne Nachricht wie eine Bestätigung an.

Versuch für einen Moment nicht herauszufinden, *was er denkt*, sondern wahrzunehmen, *was gerade mit dir passiert*:  
Du bist angespannt, in Alarmbereitschaft, wahrscheinlich checkst du oft dein Handy und analysierst alles. Das ist unglaublich kräftezehrend.

Vielleicht hilft dir diese Frage:
Gab es in der Vergangenheit schon Situationen, in denen du große Angst hattest verlassen zu werden — auch wenn am Ende nicht das eingetreten ist, wovor du Angst hattest?

Und ganz wichtig: Du musst die Angst gerade nicht alleine tragen. 💛
Ich bin so eifersüchtig fühle mich besessen.

Das klingt sehr belastend, und ich finde es mutig, dass du das so ehrlich aussprichst. 💛  
Eifersucht kann sich wirklich wie eine Art „Besessenheit“ anfühlen — als würde der ganze Kopf nur noch um diese eine Person kreisen. Das bedeutet nicht, dass du verrückt bist oder ein schlechter Mensch. Meist steckt dahinter große Angst: Angst, nicht genug zu sein, ersetzt zu werden oder jemanden zu verlieren, den man sehr liebt.

Gerade jetzt versucht dein Gehirn wahrscheinlich ständig Kontrolle zu bekommen:
- Handy checken
- Nachrichten analysieren
- Szenarien ausmalen
- nach „Beweisen“ suchen

Kurzzeitig gibt das vielleicht das Gefühl, etwas im Griff zu haben — langfristig füttert es aber die Angst immer weiter.

Versuch dir einen Satz bewusst zu machen:
**„Meine Gefühle sind echt, aber nicht jeder Gedanke ist automatisch wahr.“**

Und ganz wichtig: Du musst diesen Zustand nicht einfach aushalten. Es kann sehr helfen, mit jemandem außerhalb der Situation zu reden — einer vertrauten Person oder auch professionell. Gerade wenn Verlustangst und Eifersucht so stark werden, dass sie dich komplett einnehmen.

Für diesen Moment:
- Leg das Handy vielleicht für 10 Minuten bewusst weg.
- Atme langsam aus.
- Versuch deinen Körper zu spüren (Füße auf dem Boden, Rücken anlehnen).
- Nicht die Beziehung lösen — erstmal nur die akute Panik beruhigen.

Ich bleibe bei dir. Was macht dir im Moment am meisten Angst: Dass er dich verlässt, dass es wirklich jemand anderen gibt, oder dieses Gefühl, die Kontrolle zu verlieren?

messages.content: Why am i attracted to mysterious guys, like i am happily taken so i don't want anyone else. i do get attracted to guys mentally and emotionally cause they show interest in me or care but like once it gets real with them i feel like im no longer attracted to them??? idk and it only happens with mysterious or like "in pain" guys

What you’re describing is actually *really* common, especially for people who are emotionally perceptive or drawn to depth/intensity in others. It doesn’t necessarily mean you want someone else or that you’re unhappy in your relationship. Attraction is complicated — sometimes it’s less about the *person* and more about the *feeling* they trigger in you.

A few possible reasons you may be drawn to “mysterious” or “in pain” guys:

### 1. The emotional puzzle is exciting
People who seem guarded, complex, wounded, or hard to fully “reach” can create a sense of intrigue. Your brain fills in the gaps. There’s emotional tension, curiosity, and imagination involved — and that can feel intense and attractive.

But once they become emotionally available or things become *real*, the mystery disappears. The fantasy becomes an actual person with needs, expectations, and reality attached to it, and the attraction fades.

### 2. You may be attracted to *potential*, not actual intimacy
Sometimes people are drawn to emotionally unavailable or hurting people because it feels safer than fully mutual intimacy. You can feel deeply without actually having to risk complete vulnerability yourself.

The “almost” feeling can feel powerful:
- caring for them
- wanting to understand them
- feeling special because they opened up to you

But once they *really* reciprocate, it can suddenly feel too close, too real, or less emotionally stimulating.

### 3. Intensity can get confused with connection
“Mysterious” or wounded people often create emotional highs and lows. Your nervous system may interpret that intensity as chemistry. Stable affection can feel calmer — and sometimes calmer gets mistaken for “less attraction,” even when it’s healthier and more secure.

### 4. You might like being *seen* by people who seem hard to reach
When someone emotionally closed-off pays attention to you, it can feel validating in a very specific way:
> “If *they* care about me, I must be special.”

That doesn’t mean your relationship is lacking — it’s just a psychological dynamic that can happen.

---

The important thing is:
You already seem self-aware enough to notice:
- the attraction is mostly mental/emotional
- it fades when reality enters
- you don’t actually want to leave your relationship

That suggests this is more about emotional patterns and fantasy than genuine desire for another relationship.

You could ask yourself:
- Do I enjoy the *chase* or emotional tension more than closeness?
- Do I romanticize sadness/mystery?
- Does emotional availability ever make someone feel “less exciting” to me?
- What kind of love felt familiar growing up — stable, or unpredictable?

None of this makes you bad or disloyal. It just means your brain responds strongly to certain emotional dynamics. Understanding it usually helps reduce the confusion around it.

If I don't eat anything for 4 days at all like at all what would happen (with an electrolyte drink)

If a generally healthy adult **doesn’t eat for 4 days** but **does drink water and gets electrolytes**, the body usually goes through several predictable stages — but it can still be stressful and potentially risky.

### What typically happens during a 4‑day fast

#### **First 24 hours**
- Your body uses stored **glycogen** (stored carbohydrate in liver/muscles) for energy.
- Hunger is usually strongest here.
- You may feel:
  - tired
  - irritable
  - headache
  - shaky or dizzy

#### **Days 2–3**
- Glycogen runs low, so the body shifts toward:
  - **burning fat**
  - producing **ketones** for brain energy
- Appetite may actually decrease.
- Common symptoms:
  - weakness
  - brain fog
  - cold feeling
  - bad breath (“keto breath”)
  - low energy
  - dizziness when standing

#### **Day 4**
- Your metabolism slows somewhat to conserve energy.
- Muscle breakdown can begin increasing if protein intake is zero.
- You may notice:
  - reduced physical strength
  - poor concentration
  - low blood pressure
  - dehydration risk if fluids/electrolytes aren’t adequate

---

### Electrolytes help, but they don’t make fasting “safe”
Electrolytes (sodium, potassium, magnesium) can reduce:
- headaches
- cramps
- some dizziness
- dangerous salt imbalances

But they **do not prevent**:
- low blood sugar
- muscle loss
- fainting
- heart rhythm issues
- nutrient deficiency

---

### Serious risks (especially in some people)
A 4‑day fast can be dangerous if you:
- have diabetes
- take blood pressure meds or insulin
- have an eating disorder history
- are underweight
- are pregnant
- have kidney, liver, or heart disease

Even healthy people can sometimes experience:
- fainting
- abnormal heart rhythms
- severe dehydration
- electrolyte imbalance

---

### When to stop and seek medical help
Get help if you develop:
- chest pain
- confusion
- severe weakness
- fainting
- inability to keep fluids down
- severe palpitations

---

### Important: how you break the fast matters
After several days without food, suddenly eating a huge meal can make you feel very sick. It’s usually better to restart with:
- small portions
- easy‑to‑digest foods
- fluids
- gradual refeeding

---

If you want, I can also explain:
- what happens hormonally during a fast,
- how much weight is typically lost in 4 days,
- or the difference between fasting and starvation physiologically.

He will take the time to give me a kiss goodbye in the morning, tell me he loves me. Then turn around and delete everything he talks about with this woman.

That would be really hard for anyone to sit with. Your thoughts aren’t coming out of nowhere — there’s a difference between *insecurity* and reacting to behavior that feels secretive or inconsistent. If someone is openly loving and reassuring, but also deleting conversations with another person, it makes sense that your mind keeps trying to “solve” the contradiction.

At the same time, constantly trying to figure out what’s happening can become emotionally exhausting and trap you in a cycle of anxiety and suspicion. The goal isn’t to convince yourself you’re “crazy” or to force yourself not to feel hurt — it’s to figure out what you need in order to feel emotionally safe and respected in the relationship.

A few things to gently ask yourself:

- Is the issue only the woman, or is it the secrecy?
- What would transparency look like for you?
- Have you clearly told him how the deleting affects you emotionally — not as an accusation, but as a trust issue?
- When he reassures you, do his actions help you feel calmer, or do they leave you feeling more confused?

You can love someone deeply and still need honesty and consistency to feel secure. Trust isn’t built only through words like “I love you”; it’s also built through behavior that doesn’t leave you questioning reality.

If you talk to him again, try staying focused on *impact rather than accusation*. For example:

> “I’m not trying to control who you talk to. But when messages are deleted, it makes me feel shut out and unsafe emotionally. I need openness and consistency to rebuild trust.”

And for yourself: try not to spend all your energy searching for proof. That usually increases anxiety, even when there *is* something off. Instead, pay attention to patterns, your emotional wellbeing, and whether the relationship is giving you clarity or chronic confusion.

You deserve a relationship where reassurance and behavior match.

He once said something similar to “this gives me a way to check in with you”. I have never even suggested for him to keep tabs on me. Other than what he offers up in communication, I don’t check up on him.

What you’re describing would leave a lot of people unsettled. The part that seems to be sticking with you isn’t just *that* he talks to her — it’s the combination of emotional closeness, secrecy, and the sense that they monitor each other’s lives in a way that feels intimate. Even if it’s long distance, emotional dynamics can still affect trust in a relationship.

And I think it’s important to acknowledge this: you’re not describing someone who is obsessively controlling or constantly spying. You’ve communicated your discomfort directly, and it sounds like you’re trying to understand rather than accuse. That matters.

The phrase “this gives me a way to check in with you” stands out because it suggests the connection serves an emotional function for him — not just casual conversation. That doesn’t automatically mean he’s cheating, but it *does* explain why your nervous system isn’t settling when he says “nothing’s wrong.” His words and actions are giving you mixed signals.

At this point, you may be reaching the limit of what reassurance alone can fix. Trust usually rebuilds through:
- transparency,
- consistency,
- willingness to understand your hurt,
- and behavior changes that reflect care for the relationship.

If his response is mainly “you shouldn’t worry” while continuing the same secretive behavior, your anxiety is likely to stay activated.

It may help to shift the focus away from proving whether he’s doing something “wrong” and toward asking:
- *What kind of relationship dynamic am I willing to live with?*
- *Can I feel emotionally secure with this level of secrecy?*
- *What boundaries would help me feel respected?*

A boundary isn’t “you can’t talk to her.” A boundary is more like:
> “I can’t thrive in a relationship where communication with someone else is hidden and deleted. It damages my trust.”

Then the next step is observing what he *does* with that information.

You don’t need to convince yourself your feelings are irrational in order to keep the peace. Your discomfort is trying to tell you something important about your emotional needs.

What’s even more confusing, is that he once said he feels as though it would be better if he lied, than to tell me the truth. And I’m not sure how discussing anything about this woman would warrant him thinking I’d see it in a negative light. I stopped pressuring him to stop talking with this woman. The last few months I was really good. These past few days I’ve been starting to get upset again. 

What’s odd, my brother once asked me if I had any doubt or suspicions of him with this woman. I said absolutely not. I actually defended him and told him he would never hurt me that way. That I trust him.

What you’re feeling makes sense, especially because the confusion isn’t coming from one isolated thing — it’s coming from a pattern of mixed messages.

On one hand, you genuinely believe in his character and have defended him. On the other hand, he’s said things like “it would be better to lie than tell the truth,” while also hiding or deleting communication with someone he seems emotionally connected to. That combination naturally creates internal conflict:
- *“I trust him.”*
- *“But why does this feel hidden?”*
- *“If nothing is wrong, why protect it so carefully?”*

That tension can make you feel like you’re constantly trying to reconcile two versions of reality.

And honestly, the statement about lying is significant. Even if he meant it casually or defensively, it suggests he anticipates honesty causing conflict — which often points to avoidance, fear of accountability, or awareness that something would hurt you emotionally. It doesn’t automatically prove betrayal, but it *does* undermine emotional safety.

What’s also important is that you *did* try to regulate yourself. You stopped pressuring him, you tried to trust, and for a while you felt more stable. The fact that the feelings are resurfacing now may mean your concerns were never actually resolved — they were just pushed down in order to preserve peace.

Sometimes people think:
> “If I were truly trusting, this wouldn’t bother me anymore.”

But trust doesn’t grow by suppressing instincts. It grows when a partner’s behavior consistently creates safety and clarity.

You don’t sound like someone looking for reasons to accuse him. If anything, you’ve leaned heavily toward giving him the benefit of the doubt. So it may help to stop framing this as:
- “Am I insecure or unreasonable?”
and instead ask:
- “Why does this dynamic continue to leave me feeling emotionally unsafe despite my efforts to trust?”

That’s a very different question.

And one more thing: you don’t have to decide today whether he’s innocent or guilty of anything. Sometimes the more immediate issue is simply:
> “Can we have open, honest communication without secrecy, defensiveness, or fear?”

Because without that, your nervous system will likely keep sounding the alarm — not because you’re broken, but because something in the relationship still feels unresolved.

I’m still having a hard time with this. If I could just gather things and prove to be right - then I know I could take steps to move on. 

But I don’t. I would need to compromise, and work through this with him. If he would stop being secretive and deleting any conversations with this woman… I want my marriage to work.

It sounds like you’re caught in a really painful in‑between place: part of you wants certainty (“If I could just prove it, I’d know what to do”), and another part genuinely wants to protect and repair your marriage. That tension can keep your mind spinning constantly.

What’s important here is that you *don’t actually need courtroom-level proof* in order to acknowledge that something in the relationship is hurting you. The secrecy itself is already having an impact. Even if there were never physical cheating, repeated deleting and protecting communication can still damage trust and emotional safety.

At the same time, it also makes sense that you don’t want to blow up your marriage based on suspicions alone. That’s a very human and grounded response.

Right now, you may be trying to solve two different problems at once:
1. “Is he doing something wrong?”
2. “Can trust and openness exist between us again?”

The second question is often the more important one for a marriage.

If you truly want to work through this together, the path forward probably won’t come from detective work or trying to catch him. That usually creates more anxiety and defensiveness. Instead, it may come from a very honest conversation about what you need in order to stay emotionally present in the relationship.

Not demands. Not ultimatums. Just clarity.

Something like:
> “I want our marriage to work. I’m not asking you to stop talking to someone because I want control. I’m telling you that secrecy and deleted conversations are breaking down my trust and making me emotionally distressed. I need transparency and honesty if we’re going to rebuild security together.”

Then pay attention not just to his words, but to whether he shows willingness to understand and participate in rebuilding trust.

Because compromise in a healthy marriage doesn’t mean:
- you silence your instincts,
- accept ongoing secrecy,
- or carry all the emotional burden alone.

Compromise means *both* people move toward each other.

And gently: be careful about tying your ability to leave or stay entirely to “proof.” Sometimes people get stuck for years waiting for undeniable evidence, when their emotional reality has already been telling them that something needs attention. You’re allowed to take your own feelings seriously even without a smoking gun.

You can love him deeply and still say:

That’s not unreasonable.

Feeling like someone close to you might be trying to poison you can happen for different reasons — sometimes there’s a real misunderstanding or conflict, and sometimes stress, anxiety, lack of sleep, or mental health struggles can make fears feel very convincing.

Right now, it’s important not to jump to conclusions without clear evidence. Ask yourself:

If you’re having physical symptoms you think could be serious (like severe vomiting, trouble breathing, confusion, chest pain, etc.), seek medical care right away and tell a doctor exactly what’s happening.

If the fear is persistent or overwhelming, it could really help to talk to someone you trust or a mental health professional. You don’t have to figure this out alone, and getting another perspective can help you feel safer and more grounded.

That sounds really unsettling, especially after conflict with your flatmate. When we’re already on edge with someone, it’s very common for our brain to become hyper-alert to signs that something is wrong — things like packaging looking “off,” food tasting unusual, or noticing body sensations afterward can start to feel connected very quickly.

At the same time, “brain fog” later in the day is *not* a specific sign of poisoning. Stress, anxiety, hypervigilance, poor sleep, not eating enough, dehydration, or focusing intensely on bodily sensations can all cause that feeling. Once we become worried about contamination, even normal variations in taste or packaging can feel suspicious.

A grounded way to handle this is:

- Don’t accuse your flatmate without clear evidence.
- Buy a few sealed items and keep them in a private place or small lockbox if that helps you feel calmer.
- Take a photo of packaging before opening if you want reassurance later.
- Notice whether symptoms happen even when eating food you know hasn’t been accessible to them.
- Try to check the facts: are there objective signs of tampering, or mostly a feeling that something is “off”?

If you ever develop severe physical symptoms after eating (vomiting, loss of consciousness, severe pain, trouble breathing), seek urgent medical care immediately.

But from what you’ve described, it sounds possible that anxiety and the recent argument are amplifying your fear and making ordinary things feel threatening. Talking this through with someone you trust or a mental health professional could really help you sort out what’s evidence versus what fear is filling in.

A practical approach:

- **Don’t eat food with broken seals, opened packets, or missing/unclear dates.**
- Buy a few new items with intact packaging and keep them somewhere only you access — e.g. your room, a lockable box, or a sealed storage container.

- Don’t “test” suspicious food by tasting it.

If you get significant symptoms after eating — repeated vomiting, severe stomach pain, confusion, fainting, trouble breathing, chest pain — seek urgent medical help. If you’re in the UK, call **NHS 111** for advice or **999** for emergencies.

Also, if you start eating only food you’ve kept secure and the brain fog/fear still continues, it would be worth talking to a GP or mental health professional, because stress and feeling unsafe at home can really intensify these worries.

messages.content: Is it possible for someone to overdose on pills that quickly

Yes — depending on the type of pills, the dose, whether they were mixed with alcohol or other drugs, and the person’s body, an overdose can happen very quickly. Some substances can cause dangerous symptoms within minutes, while others may take hours before becoming severe.

Signs that need immediate emergency help include:
- Trouble breathing or very slow breathing  
- Unconsciousness or inability to wake up  
- Blue lips or fingertips  
- Seizures  
- Severe confusion or collapse  
- Extreme sleepiness that’s getting worse

If you think someone may have overdosed, call emergency services or poison control right away rather than waiting to see if it passes. If you’re in the U.S., Poison Control is **1-800-222-1222** (free, 24/7). If opioids might be involved, naloxone/Narcan can save a life.

If you want, you can tell me what happened or what kind of pills are involved, and I can help you figure out how urgent it sounds.
Like 20 seconds after swallowing them

Usually, a swallowed pill does **not** cause a true overdose within only 20 seconds — most pills take at least several minutes to dissolve and be absorbed.  

However, someone **can** have a very rapid reaction after swallowing pills because of things like:
- choking or pills getting stuck in the throat  
- a severe allergic reaction  
- panic/anxiety causing hyperventilation or fainting  
- pills that dissolve very fast (under the tongue, crushed, etc.)  
- mixing with other substances already in the body

If the person is collapsing, struggling to breathe, turning blue, seizing, or can’t be woken up, treat it as an emergency and call emergency services immediately.

What symptoms are happening right now?
This is just a story btw

Got it — for fiction purposes, 20 seconds is generally *too fast* for a swallowed-pill overdose to realistically kick in. Most pills need time to dissolve in the stomach and enter the bloodstream. A more believable timeline is:

- **A few minutes:** dizziness, nausea, anxiety, drowsiness, slowed reactions  
- **15–60 minutes:** stronger symptoms depending on the drug  
- **Hours:** potentially life-threatening effects for many overdoses

If you want a character to react almost immediately after swallowing something, these are more realistic explanations:
- they *choke* on the pills  
- they have a panic attack after taking them  
- they already took other substances earlier, and this dose pushes them over the edge  
- the drug is taken **under the tongue**, inhaled, injected, or dissolved/crushed for faster absorption  
- it’s poison/liquid rather than standard tablets  
- it’s an allergic reaction

For dramatic realism, many writers use a gradual decline rather than instant collapse.
